pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards should be learned through a progression from terminology and mental model to tracing, implementation, and independent application. Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 2. build the concept for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model

pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 3. build a mental model for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

pages.title: 4. Worked example
pages.content: Take one small example for **Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards** and solve it in visible steps: state the input, apply the first rule, update the state, and predict the output or effect. Then compare your reasoning with the executable example in this topic.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 4. worked example for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

pages.title: 5. Dry run before execution
pages.content: Trace the program line by line using a state table. Record changed variables, object fields, references, collections, thread state, or exception flow. The goal is to make the execution predictable rather than mysterious.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 5. dry run before execution for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

pages.title: 6. Guided implementation

pages.title: 8. Mastery gate

pages.title: Debugging and failure analysis
pages.content:
### Debugging Optional and Functional Error Handling

When a program fails, classify the failure before changing code:

**Compile-time:** the type or API contract is invalid.

**Runtime:** the program reaches an operation whose preconditions are violated.

**Logic:** the program runs but produces an incorrect state or output.

**Concurrency / lifecycle:** the code is valid in isolation but fails because timing, ownership, cleanup, or shared state was handled incorrectly.

- **Calling get without checking presence:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Using Optional for every field in a domain model:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Confusing orElse with orElseGet side effects:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Returning null from a method that promises Optional:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.

**Debugging loop:** reproduce -> isolate -> state the rule -> fix one cause -> rerun the smallest failing case.

pages.title: Mastery and interview review
pages.content:
### Mastery review

Before moving on, you should be able to explain **Optional and Functional Error Handling** without looking at code, implement the smallest correct version, identify one edge case, and justify one API-design choice.

**Mastery checklist**
- [ ] Use Optional to represent a possible absence explicitly.
- [ ] Chain map, filter, flatMap, orElse and orElseGet safely.
- [ ] Know when Optional improves an API and when it adds unnecessary complexity.

**Interview connection:** explain the feature in 30 seconds, give one runnable example, and name one failure mode or design trade-off.

**Transfer challenge:** change one requirement in the examples and predict what part of the implementation must change.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: Optional map
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){Optional<String>x=Optional.of("java");System.out.println(x.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("NONE"));}}
codeExamples.explanation: map transforms the contained value only when present.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: Optional filter
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){Optional<Integer>x=Optional.of(8).filter(v->v%2==0);System.out.println(x.orElse(-1));}}
codeExamples.explanation: filter keeps a present value only when the predicate passes.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: ofNullable
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){String x=null;System.out.println(Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse("UNKNOWN"));}}
codeExamples.explanation: ofNullable safely converts a nullable reference into Optional.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: orElseGet
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){Optional<String>x=Optional.empty();System.out.println(x.orElseGet(()->"generated"));}}
codeExamples.explanation: orElseGet computes the fallback only when needed.
